text: Established experience can supply context and judgment when working with AI, potentially giving incumbents an advantage if junior tasks are reassigned.
locator: Opening and experience section; S8 Findings/Limitations; S7 V.B and VI
limitations: Not a measured universal senior advantage; illustrated analyst example is hypothetical. Tenure, age and skill differ. S7 demonstrates the opposite distribution of task gains in its setting.

text: The South Korean preprint describes junior tasks moving to senior-plus-AI workflows, based on 14 interviews.
limitations: Network/purposive recruitment; not population prevalence, causal estimation or China/Malaysia evidence.

text: Liu and Wang's abstract reports increasingly selective Chinese AI recruitment, including postgraduate and one-to-five-year experience requirements.
locator: Directly inspected public ScienceDirect abstract; full text not appraised
limitations: Abstract attribution only; complete methods not appraised. Describes AI-related ads, not all graduates or hires. No causal youth-unemployment conclusion.

text: Malaysia's 2025 exposure report maps model-scored tasks to 2021 LFS employment; age shares differ by exposure group.
locator: PDF pages 14–16 zero-based; Figures 6–7 and methods
limitations: Exposure is overlap in tasks, not adoption or displacement. 2021 employment composition, not a current graduate survey.

text: Highest-exposure percentages by age 15–24 through 55–64 are 26,32,29,24,17; lowest-exposure percentages are 44,37,31,33,36.
locator: Figures 6–7 on PDF page 17 (zero-based page 16), visually inspected
limitations: Denominator is workers within each age group. Two middle categories omitted. No confidence interval or new estimate claimed.

text: The World Bank–ISIS authors identify a possible bottleneck in progression into specialised work.
limitations: Not observed individual career transitions or a finding that all young workers lose.

text: Cheng reports exposure–employment-loss associations including for ages 25–34, without causal identification or measuring first hiring.
limitations: Formal-private-sector separations; fixed LFS denominators; no firm adoption measure; no significant positive 15–24 finding.

text: Rosli argues that exposure cannot establish adoption or AI-caused losses and calls for linked adoption/outcome data.
locator: Why attribution is premature; Measure better
limitations: Commentary, not an independent causal outcome study. Critiques S3/S4; not independent replication.

text: In a 5,172-agent customer-support study, less experienced/lower-skilled employees gained more from AI assistance; most agents were based in the Philippines.
limitations: Non-random staggered rollout at one firm/subcontractors. Task productivity among employees, not graduate recruitment.

text: The authors describe AI-from-joining agents reaching about 2.5 resolutions/hour after two months; never-treated agents reached roughly that level after 8–10 months.
locator: V.B.3 Moving Down the Experience Curve, Figure V narrative
limitations: Not exact time-to-target estimates, graph digitization, individual guarantees, effect-size confidence intervals or Malaysian forecasts. The 8–10 range is descriptive.

text: The US CPS working paper finds no significant broad relative recent-graduate unemployment increase in summer 2026.
locator: Abstract and PDF pp.19–23 zero-based results/conclusions
limitations: US, bachelor’s holders ages22–25 not enrolled; no causal proof of absence or exclusion of occupation-specific harm.

text: Preserving supervised assignments and assessing verification/judgment are proposals worth testing.
limitations: No intervention or outcome evaluation run; no policy guarantee. No author personal experience asserted.
